# Back to the beginning: importing data

Most of the time, datasets will not come already loaded in R, but it can be complicated to get the data in correctly. 

For `csv` files exported from redcap, `read_csv()` from the [`readr`](https://readr.tidyverse.org) package is a good place to start.

::: {.callout-tip}
The core packages in the `tidyverse` are: `dplyr` (data cleaning),  `ggplot2` (visualization), `readr` (importing data), `forcats` (factors), `stringr` (strings), `lubridate` (times and dates), `tibble` (alternative to `data.frame`), `tidyr` (pivoting between long and wide formats), and `purrr` (dealing with functions and vectors). 
:::

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```


```{r readr}
#| eval: false
dat <- read_csv("somedata.csv")
```

If you export the dataset with decimal points, `.`, you'll find that `read_csv()` should work just fine. If you exported it with decimal commas, `,`, or if you've saved data in Excel on your computer using, say, a Swiss locale, try `read_csv2()`. Find out more about `read_csv()` in [R4DS](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-import.html), and more about locales in [the `readr` documentation](https://readr.tidyverse.org/articles/locales.html).

::: {.callout-tip}
Why not `read.csv()`?
:::

If you are not exporting data from redcap or another electronic data capture system, consider organizing your data to enable efficient data analysis @broman.

If you're working with an Excel spreadsheet, `.xlsx`, the [`readxl`](https://readxl.tidyverse.org) package will help. 

For formats from other statistical programs (for example from SPSS, SAS, or STATA), try the [`haven`](https://haven.tidyverse.org) package.
